title: Temperature
objectives: Divide the logits by a temperature and see the trade between safe and varied samples.

screens.title: Three lists

screens.prose: Before softmax, divide the logits by a **temperature** $T$. The bars show the model’s first-letter chances after `...` at three temperatures.

screens.question: At $T = 0.5$, what chance does a get? Give a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Move the slider to 0.5 and read a.

byKey.t1: That is at $T = 1$. Move the slider to 0.5.

explain.text: Halving the temperature doubles every logit, so the favourite pulls away: a goes from 0.1502 to 0.3342. At $T = 2$ the bars level out and a drops to 0.0831.

screens.title: Temperature as a power
screens.prose: Name it: sampling at temperature $T$ uses $\operatorname{softmax}(z/T)$, which is each chance raised to the power $1/T$ and rescaled. $T < 1$ sharpens, $T > 1$ flattens. If you met AI basics, its “temperature 1/2 squares the chances” is $T = \tfrac12$.
screens.question: Chances 0.5, 0.3 and 0.2 at $T = \tfrac12$: what does the first become? Give a decimal to 4 places.

hints.text: Square each chance, then divide by their sum.

byKey.noscale: You squared but did not rescale: the chances must add to 1.
byKey.root: That is $T = 2$: square roots flatten. $T = \tfrac12$ squares.

explain.text: $e^{z/T} = (e^{z})^{1/T}$, so dividing logits by $\tfrac12$ squares the chances: 0.25, 0.09 and 0.04, which rescale to 0.6579, 0.2368 and 0.1053.

screens.title: The two limits
screens.prose: As $T \to 0$ the largest logit takes all the chance: sampling becomes argmax. As $T$ grows, every logit over $T$ shrinks toward 0. At $T = 100$ the MLP’s dev loss is 3.2674.

state.caption: The supplied MLP on the dev names with its logits divided by T.

screens.question: What loss does a very large $T$ approach?

options.why: Large $T$ throws away what the model knows; 0 needs every chance to be 1.
Only $T = 1$ keeps the model as trained.

hints.text: What are the chances when every logit is near 0?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Picture all logits divided by a huge number.

explain.text: Huge $T$ makes all logits near 0, so every symbol gets $\tfrac{1}{27}$ and the loss tends to $\ln 27 = 3.2958$; at $T = 100$ it is 3.2674. Tiny $T$ gives argmax, the one-name sampler of l9.

screens.title: Which T fits best?
screens.prose: Divide the trained MLP’s logits by $T$ and score the dev names. The table gives the dev loss for several $T$.

state.caption: The supplied MLP on the dev names with its logits divided by T.

screens.question: Which temperature gives the least dev loss among those listed?

feedback.correct: $T = 1$, 2.1609; a finer search finds the least at 1.01, only 0.00007 lower.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Pick the least dev loss.

explain.text: The trained model minimised cross-entropy on training names, so $T = 1$ is close to best on dev too: 2.1609. A grid in steps of 0.01 puts the least at 1.01, a difference of 0.00007 nats, within noise.

screens.title: A different model?
screens.prose: A learner says: “at $T = 0.5$ the model writes better names, so it has become a better model.”

hints.text: Only the division by $T$ before softmax; the weights did not move.

feedback.correct: The weights are unchanged; as a model of names it is worse: 2.5456 against 2.1609.

byKey.right: You judged by a handful of samples. The dev loss says the model at $T = 0.5$ predicts names worse.

explain.text: $T$ divides the logits after the network has run; the weights do not change. Safer names come at a cost: at $T = 0.5$ the dev loss is 2.5456, because real names include the rarer letters it now starves.

screens.question: At $T = 1$, what chance does the model give a as a first letter? Give a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. At $T = 1$ the logits are unchanged.

explain.text: Dividing by 1 changes no logit, so the chances are the model’s own: a 0.1502. Every loss in this course was measured at $T = 1$.

widget.how: Submit runs 6 hidden tests: T = 1 and T = 0.5 on three logits (rounded to 6 places), and two rows with logits near 2,000 at T = 2. Then a tiny T (nearly one-hot), a huge T (nearly 1/27 each), and rows of 27 that add to 1.

mutants.symptom: Multiplies by T, so a low temperature flattens instead of sharpening.
No maximum taken out: exp(500) overflows.
Normalises over the whole array, not each row.

hints.text: Divide by `T` first, then subtract each row’s maximum.
`z.max(axis=-1, keepdims=True)` and `e.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True)` keep it row by row.

feedback.correct: Your softmax handles every temperature, both limits and huge logits.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Read the first failing test.

byKey.test-2: At $T = 0.5$ the chances sharpen: divide the logits by T, do not multiply.
byKey.test-3: Subtract each row’s maximum before `exp`: 2,000 over 2 is 1,000, and `exp(1000)` overflows.

explain.text: Divide by $T$, subtract each row’s maximum, exponentiate and normalise each row. The subtraction changes nothing mathematically and keeps `exp` finite.

screens.title: Scenarios for a risk report
screens.prose: A risk team samples 1,000 market scenarios from a generative model of daily moves to fill a report on tail losses. To make the scenarios look “realistic”, someone sets the temperature to 0.5.
screens.question: What does that do to the report?

options.text: It makes the report more accurate
options.why: More typical scenarios, but a tail report needs the rare ones at their true chance.

options.text: Nothing: the model is the same
options.why: The model is the same, but the samples are not drawn from it any more.

hints.text: What happens to small chances at $T = 0.5$?
They are squared: a chance of 1% becomes about 0.01%, before rescaling.

feedback.correct: It starves the tails, so the report understates tail risk.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask what $T < 1$ does to rare outcomes.

byKey.better: You preferred typical scenarios. A tail-loss report is about the rare ones, which $T = 0.5$ suppresses.

explain.text: $T = \tfrac12$ squares every chance before rescaling, so a rare crash day becomes far rarer still. A report on tail losses needs $T = 1$, the model’s own chances.

ideas: Sampling at temperature $T$ uses $\operatorname{softmax}(z/T)$: each chance to the power $1/T$, rescaled. $T < 1$ sharpens, $T > 1$ flattens.
$T \to 0$ is argmax; very large $T$ tends to equal chances and a loss of $\ln 27$. The MLP’s dev loss is least near $T = 1$ (2.1609).
Temperature changes how we sample, not the model: low $T$ writes safe, plain names and starves rare outcomes.
summary.trap: Thinking a low temperature makes a better model, or choosing $T$ by how a few samples look.

quiz.question: What does a temperature below 1 do to the chances?

options.text: Sharpens them: likely symbols gain, rare ones lose
Nothing, unless the model is retrained
options.why: It acts at sampling time, on the logits.

explain.text: Dividing logits by $T < 1$ stretches their differences, so the favourite gains.

quiz.question: What does the first become at $T = \tfrac12$? Give a decimal to 4 places.

explain.text: Squares 0.36 and 0.16 add to 0.52, so the first becomes $0.36 / 0.52 = 0.6923$.

quiz.question: How should a temperature be chosen for a model that will be judged on dev loss?

options.text: By how good a few samples look
options.why: A few samples are noise, and looking good favours plain names, not true chances.

options.text: As low as possible, for the safest names
options.why: Low $T$ raises the dev loss: 2.5456 at 0.5.

explain.text: The dev loss rewards true chances; for the supplied MLP it is least near $T = 1$ (2.1609).
